title: Climate Champions
description: Step into the shoes of a teenage environmental activist fighting to save a local forest from a corporate development project. Every decision affects your community support, resources, and real-world impact.
learning_objectives: Understand how collective action builds community power
Develop ethical reasoning when personal cost meets public good
Practice adapting strategies when plans face resistance
Recognise the difference between short-term wins and long-term impact
Build confidence in speaking truth to institutional power
learning_concept: Real change requires more than passion — it demands strategy, persistence, and the courage to keep showing up even when progress is invisible.
psychological_framework: Systems Thinking and Civic Agency — understanding how individual action connects to collective change within complex social and political systems

chapters.title: The Problem
chapters.teaser: A beloved forest near your school is about to be bulldozed — can you stop it?

chapters.teaser: Your movement is growing — but so is the opposition...

chapters.teaser: The forest's fate is decided — but the movement you built will outlast this fight.

A designated natural area managed collaboratively by local communities to protect and restore native plant and animal species.
Employment in sectors that contribute to preserving or restoring environmental quality, such as conservation, renewable energy, and eco-tourism.

scenes.title: The Notice Board
scenes.narrative: On the notice board outside your school in Pune, someone has pinned a municipal notice: 'Proposed development — Sinhagad Road Forest Patch (8.3 hectares) to be cleared for IT Park and commercial complex. Public comment period: 14 days.' You've played in that forest your whole childhood — found insects for science projects there, had your first heartbreak there. And now a corporation wants to pave it over. Your classmate Tanvi grabs your arm: 'We have to do something.'
scenes.image_prompt: Two Indian teenagers reading a government notice pinned to a school board, expressions shifting from shock to determination, urban Indian school exterior, late afternoon sunlight, photorealistic
scenes.coaching_moment: The first step in any movement is choosing to care. Awareness without action changes nothing — but action without awareness wastes energy.
scenes.reflection_prompt: What would it take for you to stand up publicly against a decision made by adults with more power than you?

scenes.title: The Opposition
scenes.narrative: The IT park developer, Apex Infra Ltd., is not sitting still. They've put up glossy banners around the area: '5,000 jobs. Modern infrastructure. Progress for Pune.' Some of your neighbours — especially those who've been unemployed — are nodding along. Your aunt says quietly, 'Beta, sometimes we need jobs more than trees.' You feel the sting of that. The issue is no longer black and white. How do you respond to people who genuinely need those jobs?
scenes.image_prompt: Indian teenager looking at corporate development banners promising jobs, neighbours watching thoughtfully, urban street in Pune, complex emotional scene, photorealistic
scenes.coaching_moment: Real environmental leadership means listening to the community's economic reality — not just preaching at it. Empathy builds bridges; judgment builds walls.

choices.label: Acknowledge the jobs argument publicly and propose an alternative site for the IT park
choices.description: Address their concern directly and offer a real solution.

choices.label: Stay focused on the environment — the job numbers are exaggerated anyway
choices.description: Don't get distracted by corporate spin.
choices.counterfactual_feedback: You optimize for resilience, but at this moment the scene asks you to lead with ethical reasoning. Don't get distracted by corporate spin.

scenes.title: The Media Moment
scenes.narrative: A local journalist from Pune Mirror calls you. She's writing a story about the forest controversy and wants a student quote. This is your first real media moment. If you say too much you might misrepresent the movement or say something that gets twisted out of context. If you say too little, you miss the chance to amplify your campaign to thousands of readers. Your heart is hammering as you hold the phone.
scenes.image_prompt: A nervous but determined Indian teenage girl holding a phone for a media interview, friends watching supportively in the background, school grounds, photorealistic
scenes.coaching_moment: Every public statement is a strategic choice. Being clear, honest, and concise in the media builds credibility that amplifies your message far beyond what you can say.

choices.label: Speak clearly and stick to three main facts: biodiversity, heritage, and alternative sites
choices.description: Prepared and focused. Let the facts do the work.
choices.counterfactual_feedback: You optimize for strategic thinking, but at this moment the scene asks you to lead with ethical reasoning. Prepared and focused. Let the facts do the work.

choices.label: Speak from the heart — tell your personal story about the forest
choices.description: Emotional authenticity cuts through in ways data cannot.

scenes.title: Going Viral — For the Wrong Reasons
scenes.narrative: The Pune Mirror article is published with the headline: 'Student Activists vs. 5000 Jobs.' Half the comments support you; the other half are furious. Someone posts a meme mocking you as 'Pune's Greta Thunberg' — and it spreads faster than your petition. Tanvi is excited: 'Controversy gets attention!' But a local councillor's aide calls to warn you: 'Stop being so aggressive, or you'll lose the swing votes on the council.'
scenes.image_prompt: Indian teenager scrolling through mixed social media reactions on a phone, some supportive, some hostile, looking conflicted, bedroom setting late at night, photorealistic
scenes.coaching_moment: Controversy creates visibility, but trust is what creates change. Long-term movements are built on credibility, not just noise.

choices.label: Respond to the meme with humour — don't let trolls define your narrative
choices.description: Defuse the tension and reclaim the story.

choices.label: Go quiet on social media and focus on direct council outreach instead
choices.description: Ignore the noise. Work where it actually matters.

scenes.title: The Alliance
scenes.narrative: A well-known environmental NGO, Green Canopy India, contacts you. They want to co-brand the campaign with their logo, bring in legal support, and mobilise their 40,000 followers. The catch: they want creative control and want to file the legal case themselves, effectively sidelining you as the student voice. It's a massive resource boost — but you worry it will become 'their' campaign, not yours.
scenes.image_prompt: Indian students meeting with professional NGO representatives in a modern conference room, discussing a collaboration with documents on the table, empowered yet cautious expressions, photorealistic
scenes.coaching_moment: Partnerships multiply impact — but only if boundaries and credit are clearly negotiated upfront. Know what you are gaining and what you might lose.
scenes.reflection_prompt: When is it worth sharing control of something you created to make it bigger?

choices.label: Accept the partnership but negotiate a student co-leadership clause
choices.description: Take the resources without losing your voice.

choices.label: Decline — you want this to remain a student-led movement
choices.description: Authenticity over resources. Stay independent.
choices.counterfactual_feedback: You optimize for resilience, but at this moment the scene asks you to lead with ethical reasoning. Authenticity over resources. Stay independent.

expert_pick.reason: Best aligns with the dimensions this scene rewards: ethical reasoning.

scenes.title: The Council Member
scenes.narrative: You get a surprise invitation to meet Councillor Meenakshi Rao, who holds the deciding vote on the development proposal. She is sympathetic — her own children used to play in that forest — but she is facing intense pressure from the party's industrial donors. 'Give me something I can take to my party,' she says. 'Data, a viable economic alternative, anything. Come to me with a credible proposal by 8 PM tonight and I will consider it seriously.'
scenes.image_prompt: Indian teenage activist sitting across from a senior female councillor in a government office, serious but hopeful conversation, late afternoon light through venetian blinds, photorealistic
scenes.coaching_moment: Decision-makers need political cover to do the right thing. Your job is to make it easier for them to say yes than to say no.

choices.label: Pull together a rigorous proposal with economic data tonight — even if it means no sleep
choices.description: Go all-in on the one person who can change the outcome.
choices.counterfactual_feedback: You optimize for delayed gratification, but at this moment the scene asks you to lead with ethical reasoning. Go all-in on the one person who can change the outcome.

choices.description: Political weight comes in numbers too.

expert_pick.reason: Best aligns with the dimensions this scene rewards: ethical reasoning.

scenes.title: The Council Chamber
scenes.narrative: The municipal council chamber is packed. Behind you sit 150 residents, several of your teachers, and a handful of journalists. In front of you, nine councillors sit in a row, with Meenakshi Rao third from the left. The developer's lawyer presents first — slick slides, job numbers, tax revenue projections. Then it is your turn. The room goes quiet. You stand up, hands slightly trembling, and face the council.
scenes.image_prompt: A young Indian girl standing at a speaker's podium in a formal municipal council chamber, facing seated councillors, a packed public gallery behind her, nervous and determined, dramatic lighting, photorealistic
scenes.coaching_moment: Your voice, grounded in truth and backed by evidence, is a legitimate form of power in a democracy. Fear is normal. Speaking anyway is courage.

choices.label: Lead with the biodiversity data and the proposed alternative site
choices.description: Facts and solutions — the most credible combination.
choices.counterfactual_feedback: You optimize for strategic thinking, but at this moment the scene asks you to lead with ethical reasoning. Facts and solutions — the most credible combination.

choices.label: Open with the personal testimonials — stories move people where data cannot
choices.description: Make the councillors see faces, not statistics.

choices.label: Directly address Councillor Rao and ask for a transparent vote on record
choices.description: Political accountability is its own kind of pressure.
choices.counterfactual_feedback: You optimize for risk tolerance, but at this moment the scene asks you to lead with ethical reasoning. Political accountability is its own kind of pressure.

expert_pick.reason: Best aligns with the dimensions this scene rewards: ethical reasoning.

scenes.title: The Twist
scenes.narrative: After your presentation, the developer's lawyer stands up with a surprise: a revised proposal that promises to preserve 30% of the forest as a 'green corridor' — a token compromise clearly designed to split your coalition. Some residents whisper that it might be 'good enough'. Tanvi hisses at you: 'Don't fall for it — 70% is still destroyed.' But others are less certain, including Councillor Rao, who looks hopefully at you.
scenes.image_prompt: A tense moment in a council chamber, developer and activist sides visible, some residents whispering and uncertain, one young activist standing firm, dramatic light, photorealistic
scenes.coaching_moment: A partial victory offered to divide your coalition is not a compromise — it is a tactic. Recognising the difference between genuine negotiation and strategic concession is essential.
scenes.reflection_prompt: At what point does accepting a compromise become surrendering your core goal?

choices.label: Reject the 30% offer publicly — it is not sufficient and you will say so
choices.description: Hold the line. Partial wins can become permanent defeats.
choices.counterfactual_feedback: You optimize for resilience, but at this moment the scene asks you to lead with ethical reasoning. Hold the line. Partial wins can become permanent defeats.

choices.label: Counter-propose 70% forest preservation as the minimum acceptable compromise
choices.description: Show you can negotiate without abandoning your core goal.

expert_pick.reason: Best aligns with the dimensions this scene rewards: ethical reasoning.

scenes.title: The Vote
scenes.narrative: The council votes. Six in favour of the original development. Two opposed. Councillor Rao raises her hand — and the room holds its breath. She votes against the development in its current form and calls for an environmental impact assessment before any further action. The forest is not saved permanently, but it has a fighting chance. Outside, residents cheer. Tanvi is crying. You feel, for the first time, what it means to change something.
scenes.image_prompt: Young Indian activists celebrating outside a municipal building at dusk, hugging each other, residents joining in, relief and joy visible, hope in the air, photorealistic
scenes.coaching_moment: Civic change rarely happens in one clean victory — it happens in increments, through showing up, persisting, and trusting the process even when the outcome is uncertain.

choices.label: 'We won a battle — now we have to win the war by staying organised'

scenes.title: The Environmental Impact Assessment
scenes.narrative: The municipal council's order for an Environmental Impact Assessment has created a 90-day window. The independent assessor, Dr. Meena Iyer, arrives from IISc Bangalore. She is thorough, impartial, and intimidating. She tells you frankly: 'Student activism got you here. Science will determine what happens next. I need you to organise community data — species counts, water table levels, historical usage patterns. Can your team deliver?' You look at Tanvi. This is no longer about signs and slogans. This is fieldwork.

scenes.coaching_moment: Passion opens doors. Evidence keeps them open. The transition from activist to advocate requires adding rigour to your conviction.

choices.label: Organise a weekend biodiversity survey with science teachers and student volunteers
choices.description: Mobilise the school's intellectual resources. Real data, real credibility.
choices.counterfactual_feedback: You optimize for strategic thinking, but at this moment the scene asks you to lead with ethical reasoning. Mobilise the school's intellectual resources. Real data, real credibility.

choices.label: Partner with the university's ecology department for professional-grade data collection
choices.description: Academic partnership adds weight and rigour to the findings.

choices.label: Focus on documenting community stories — how residents use and depend on the forest daily
choices.description: Qualitative evidence has power that spreadsheets cannot replicate.
choices.counterfactual_feedback: You optimize for empathy, but at this moment the scene asks you to lead with ethical reasoning. Qualitative evidence has power that spreadsheets cannot replicate.

scenes.title: The Counter-Campaign
scenes.narrative: Apex Infra has not been idle. They have launched a slick counter-campaign: a website called 'Pune Deserves Jobs' with testimonials from unemployed youth who want the IT park. Worse, they have found a former teacher from your school who publicly criticises the student campaign as 'naive idealism that costs real families real jobs.' The criticism stings because it contains a grain of truth. Some families in your own neighbourhood genuinely need those jobs. Tanvi is rattled for the first time.
scenes.image_prompt: Indian teenagers looking at a corporate counter-campaign website on a laptop, one looking discouraged, another looking determined, bedroom setting, evening, photorealistic
scenes.coaching_moment: When your opponent uses real people's real pain against you, the only honest response is to acknowledge that pain — and then show a better path.
scenes.reflection_prompt: How do you fight for your cause without dismissing the legitimate needs of those who disagree with you?

choices.label: Develop a counter-proposal: a green jobs plan that creates employment through forest conservation and eco-tourism
choices.description: Answer the jobs argument with a better jobs argument.

choices.label: Meet the unemployed youth from the counter-campaign and listen to their concerns directly
choices.description: Bridge-building starts with showing up where the opposition lives.
choices.counterfactual_feedback: You optimize for empathy, but at this moment the scene asks you to lead with ethical reasoning. Bridge-building starts with showing up where the opposition lives.

expert_pick.reason: Best aligns with the dimensions this scene rewards: ethical reasoning.

scenes.title: The Assessment Results
scenes.narrative: Dr. Meena Iyer's report lands like a thunderbolt. The forest contains 14 species of birds found nowhere else in urban Pune, a water table that supplies three nearby wells, and root systems preventing soil erosion on the hillside above a residential colony of 2,000 people. Removing the forest would create a measurable flood risk. The data is unambiguous. But the report also notes that the forest is 'not pristine' — it has degraded edges from encroachment. Apex Infra immediately focuses on the degradation language to argue for partial development. The fight is not over.
scenes.image_prompt: Indian teenager reading an environmental assessment report with mixed findings, highlighted sections, both hope and concern visible, school library setting, photorealistic
scenes.coaching_moment: Scientific evidence rarely delivers a clean victory. It provides ammunition for both sides. What matters is whether you use it with integrity or selectivity.

choices.label: Present the full report honestly — including the degradation findings — and argue for restoration, not just preservation
choices.description: Intellectual honesty strengthens your position more than cherry-picking ever could.

choices.label: Focus the public messaging on the flood risk data — it is the most compelling safety argument
choices.description: Lead with what moves people most. Safety trumps biodiversity in public debate.
choices.counterfactual_feedback: You optimize for strategic thinking, but at this moment the scene asks you to lead with ethical reasoning. Lead with what moves people most. Safety trumps biodiversity in public debate.

expert_pick.reason: Best aligns with the dimensions this scene rewards: ethical reasoning.

scenes.title: The Final Council Session
scenes.narrative: The municipal council reconvenes for the final vote on the Sinhagad Road forest. Armed with the EIA report, your green jobs proposal, and 4,000 petition signatures, you present your case one last time. But Apex Infra has also brought reinforcements: a revised proposal that preserves 50% of the forest and develops the degraded half. Two councillors who supported you last time are wavering. The vote will be close — perhaps decided by a single councillor.
scenes.image_prompt: Young Indian activist presenting at a packed municipal council session, charts and data visible, tense atmosphere, journalists and residents watching, photorealistic
scenes.coaching_moment: In the final moment, your credibility is built on everything you did before you walked into the room. There are no shortcuts to earned trust.

choices.label: Accept the 50% compromise — half the forest saved is better than an uncertain vote on the full forest
choices.description: A pragmatic victory. Not everything, but something real.

choices.label: Reject the compromise and push for full protection — the EIA data supports it
choices.description: All or nothing. The evidence is on your side.
choices.counterfactual_feedback: You optimize for resilience, but at this moment the scene asks you to lead with ethical reasoning. All or nothing. The evidence is on your side.

expert_pick.reason: Best aligns with the dimensions this scene rewards: ethical reasoning.

scenes.title: The Unexpected Ally
scenes.narrative: As the debate reaches its peak, someone unexpected stands up from the public gallery: Rajesh Khanna, a retired Apex Infra engineer who helped survey the original development site. He holds up a document. 'I was part of the original geological survey team,' he says. 'The soil composition data in the development proposal was modified. I have the original report.' The room explodes. Councillor Rao calls for an immediate investigation. The development proposal is suspended pending review.
scenes.image_prompt: Retired Indian engineer standing up in a council meeting holding documents, shocked reactions around the room, dramatic turning point, photorealistic
scenes.coaching_moment: Movements that build on truth eventually attract truth-tellers. When you create a space where honesty is valued, people with important information feel safe coming forward.

choices.label: Thank Rajesh publicly and call for whistleblower protection for anyone with further evidence
choices.description: Protect the truth-teller. Set a precedent for transparency.

choices.label: Use the momentum to push for immediate permanent forest protection — while the council is sympathetic
choices.description: Strike while the iron is hot. Secure the win now.
choices.counterfactual_feedback: You optimize for strategic thinking, but at this moment the scene asks you to lead with ethical reasoning. Strike while the iron is hot. Secure the win now.

expert_pick.reason: Best aligns with the dimensions this scene rewards: ethical reasoning.

scenes.title: The Planting
scenes.narrative: Six months later. The forest has been designated a Community Biodiversity Reserve — the first in Pune's history. The development proposal was permanently shelved after the geological data fraud investigation. You and Tanvi stand at the edge of the forest with 200 volunteers, planting native saplings to restore the degraded sections. Dr. Meena Iyer is there too, supervising the species selection. A reporter asks you how it feels. You look at the forest — your forest, everyone's forest — and you think of the notice board where it all started.
scenes.image_prompt: Indian teenagers and community volunteers planting saplings at the edge of a forest, banners celebrating the biodiversity reserve designation, joyful and purposeful atmosphere, golden hour, photorealistic
scenes.coaching_moment: The greatest victories in civic life are not the ones that make headlines — they are the ones that make forests. What you planted today will outlive every person in this story.

choices.label: 'This was never about one forest. It was about proving that young people can change what adults accept as inevitable'
choices.description: The lesson that transcends this fight and fuels the next one.
choices.ending_message: The Sinhagad Road forest stands. Not because of one petition, one vote, or one council session — but because a group of teenagers refused to accept that the world was not theirs to change. You built a coalition, gathered evidence, faced corporate power, and won. The saplings you planted will grow for a hundred years. So will the lesson.
choices.counterfactual_feedback: You optimize for resilience, but at this moment the scene asks you to lead with ethical reasoning. The lesson that transcends this fight and fuels the next one.

choices.label: 'I learned that the environment is not separate from jobs, heritage, or justice — it is connected to all of them'
choices.description: Systems thinking earned through real-world experience.
choices.ending_message: You did not just save a forest — you learned how environmental justice connects to economic justice, community trust, and democratic accountability. That understanding will make you a more effective advocate for the rest of your life. The forest is the proof. You are the product.

expert_pick.reason: Best aligns with the dimensions this scene rewards: ethical reasoning.

coaching_moment: Real change requires more than passion — it demands strategy, persistence, and the courage to keep showing up even when progress is invisible.
cultural_context: India is among the world's most climate-vulnerable nations, with 40% of its population dependent on rain-fed agriculture. Environmental ethics and climate action are increasingly part of India's school curricula under NEP 2020.

hallmarks: Builds coalitions before issuing demands — power flows from organized people, not solo posts
Tests one idea at a time and learns from the response, instead of broadcasting many
Distinguishes performative outrage from action that actually moves a decision-maker
Stays with the unglamorous work — meetings, paperwork, follow-up — when momentum dies
Names the stakeholders who matter (regulator, school board, neighbors) instead of fighting on social media
Optimizes for likes and shares instead of meetings that move policy
Picks a fight before figuring out who actually has the authority to change things
Treats opposition as enemies instead of as people to be persuaded
Burns out on Day 3 because they treated this as a sprint, not a campaign
Confuses being right with being effective
